steps.title: Give a value a name
steps.text:
A **value** is a piece of data. `4` is a number. `"Desk"` is text (a **string**). `true` and `false` are the two **boolean** values.

A **variable** is a name for a value:

```typescript
const opening = 4;
let open = opening;
```

- `const` gives a fixed name its value. `let` gives a name that can be assigned a new value later.
- Read `=` as "gets". A semicolon ends a statement, and statements run from top to bottom.

steps.title: Trace the count

steps.title: Join text
steps.text: For numbers, `-` subtracts. For text, `+` joins the pieces in order, and the spaces inside the quotes become part of the result.

steps.title: Find the error
steps.text:
TypeScript uses the first value to work out a type (**inference**). In `let count = 4`, `count` can only ever hold a number. Writing `: number` after the name would state the type yourself (an **annotation**).

lessons.intro: An array holds values in order. A tuple is an array with a fixed number of slots, where each slot has its own type.

steps.title: Walk through every value
steps.text:
An array holds any number of values of one type, in order.

- `number[]` is an array of numbers. `[]` is an empty array.
- `values.length` counts the entries.
- `for (const value of values)` visits each entry once, first to last.
- A variable declared before the loop can collect a result across visits. This is an accumulator.
- To build a new array, start from `[]` and call `push(value)` to add to the end.

steps.title: Fixed slots with tuples
steps.text:
Sometimes a function needs to return two results together, such as a width and a height. A tuple type lists each slot.

- `[number, string]` has exactly two slots: a `number` first, then a `string`.
- `const size: [number, number] = [1920, 1080]` is a tuple of two numbers.
- Read slots by position, `size[0]` and `size[1]`, or unpack them with `const [width, height] = size`.
- Asking for a slot that is not there, such as `size[2]`, is a type error.

TypeScript infers `number[]` for `[1920, 1080]` unless you write the tuple type. Write it on a function's return type so callers know there are exactly two slots.

lessons.intro: A value can be missing. TypeScript makes you say where that can happen, then makes you check before you use it.

steps.title: Keep missing values distinct
steps.text:
TypeScript has two "missing" values.

- `undefined` means nothing was set. Reading a field that is not there gives `undefined`.
- `null` means "deliberately empty". You write it yourself.
- `nickname?: string` marks a field as optional. Its type becomes `string | undefined`.
- `number | null` (a union) allows either a number or `null`.
- `a ?? b` gives `b` only when `a` is `null` or `undefined` (**nullish**). Otherwise it gives `a`.

Missing is not the same as empty. `0` and `""` are real values, and your code should keep them.

lessons.intro: A union type lists the kinds of value something can be. A literal type allows one exact value. Together they let the type checker reject values your code does not handle.

steps.title: One of several types
steps.text:
A union is written with `|`.

- `string | string[]` is either one string or an array of strings.
- `"S" | "M" | "L"` is a union of literal types. Only those three strings fit.
- `type Size = "S" | "M" | "L"` gives the union a name.

Before you use a union value, check which kind it is (narrowing). After the check, TypeScript knows the narrower type inside that branch.

- `typeof x === "string"` checks for a string.
- `Array.isArray(x)` checks for an array.
- `x === "S"` checks for one literal.

- `unknown` holds anything, but you cannot read fields until you check what it is. This is the safe choice.

- A **boundary case** is an input right where a rule changes, such as exactly at a limit. Bugs often live there.

- An expected miss is a normal return value, such as `null` or `{ kind: "error" }`. Callers handle it like any other result.

lessons.intro: Some work finishes later, such as reading a file or calling a server. A promise stands for a result that is not ready yet. `await` waits for it.

steps.title: Wait for a result
steps.text:
- A promise ends in one of two ways. It **resolves** with a value, or it **rejects** with a reason (like a throw).
- `Promise<string>` is a promise that resolves with a string.
- An `async` function always returns a promise, even when it returns a plain value.
- Inside an `async` function, `await promise` pauses until the promise settles. It gives the value, or throws the rejection at that line, so a `try` and `catch` around the `await` handles a rejection.

The examples and tasks here use local data, with no network or timers.

```typescript
const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([loadUser(), loadPosts()]);
```

- `Promise.all` resolves with an array of results, in the same order as the input, not the order they finished.
- If any promise rejects, `Promise.all` rejects too.
- Use one `await` after another when a step needs the previous result. Use `Promise.all` when it does not.

lessons.intro: TypeScript ships generic types that build new types from old ones (utility types). You met `Pick`, `Omit` and `Partial` in Generics. This module adds four more.

steps.title: Four more utility types
steps.text:
- `Record<K, V>` is an object with exactly the keys `K`, each holding a `V`. `Record<"fruit" | "veg", number>` means `{ fruit: number; veg: number }`.
- `Required<T>` removes every `?`, so all fields must be present. It is the opposite of `Partial<T>`.
- `Readonly<T>` marks every field `readonly`. The fields can be read but not reassigned.
- `ReturnType<typeof f>` is the type that function `f` returns. You write the function once and get its type for free.

Like all types, these only exist while checking. `Readonly` does not freeze an object at runtime.

lessons.intro: `Partial`, `Pick` and `Record` are not magic. They are written in TypeScript with three tools: `keyof`, mapped types and conditional types. This module shows how to write your own.

steps.title: Keys as a type
steps.text:
- `keyof T` is a union of `T`'s keys. For `type Point = { x: number; y: number }`, `keyof Point` is `"x" | "y"`.
- `T[K]` is the type of field `K` (an indexed access type). `Point["x"]` is `number`.
- Together they type a function that reads any field: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`.

steps.title: Make a type for every key
steps.text:
A mapped type builds an object type by going through a set of keys:

```typescript
type Optional<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };
```

Read it as: for each key `K` of `T`, make an optional field with the same type as before. That is exactly how `Partial` is written. You can change the field type too: `{ [K in keyof T]: string }` makes every field a `string`.

steps.title: Choose a type with a condition
steps.text:
A conditional type picks one of two types, like `? :` for values:

```typescript
type Kind<T> = T extends string ? "text" : "other";
```

- `T extends string` asks: does `T` fit `string`?
- `infer` names part of a type inside the check. `T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T` means "if `T` is an array, give its item type `U`, else `T`".

tasks.title: Find the item type of an array
tasks.prompt: Write the conditional type `ItemOf<T>`. When `T` is an array, it is the array's item type: `ItemOf<string[]>` is `string`. Any other type stays as it is: `ItemOf<number>` is `number`. Only the type is checked.
hints: `T extends X ? A : B` picks `A` when `T` fits `X`, else `B`.
`infer U` names a type inside the pattern, as in `(infer U)[]`.
When `T` is not an array, give back `T` itself.
tasks.starter: type ItemOf<T> = T;
tasks.solution: type ItemOf<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T;
